newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE-Australian winemaker pulls the plug on corks.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Australian winemaker pulls the plug on corks.

text.p: For some wine buffs, the whole process can be as satisfying as the drink itself: the pop as the bottle is opened, the quick sniff of the cork, the serious sipping of the wine for any taint.
But that may all be a thing of the past if a trial in Australia by the country's biggest winemaker, Southcorp Wines, can prove that synthetic corks are as good -- and as lovable -- as the real thing.
Southcorp's aim is to eliminate cork taint which can make wine smell and taste, as one industry figure put it, "like a wet washcloth that sits on the bath for a week in winter".

Taint, which manifests itself in a number of ways, is caused mostly by the compound 2,4,6 trichloroanisole (TCA) in natural cork and is the bane of the Portuguese industry which supplies the corks for most of the estimated 14 billion wine bottles filled each year around the world.

"Where the issue becomes of real concern to us, is that 99 percent of consumers do not know what the hell cork taint is," Steward Gregor, wine information manager of premium wine producer Mildara Blass, owned by the Fosters' Brewing Group, told Reuters.
"So they taste the wine and they just do not like it, so they will not buy it again," he said.
NINE BILLION PLASTIC CORKS

After a successful trial run, Southcorp, a division of Southcorp Holdings Ltd, is about to introduce a polyethylene cork developed by its sister company Southcorp Packaging in an initial run of over one million bottles of commercial wines -- the cheaper non-premium bottled varieties.

Southcorp Packaging estimates the world market for plastic corks for commercial wines at nine billion units a year, worth up to A$70 million (US$55 million) annually, and at 150 million units in Australia and New Zealand alone.
And Southcorp Wines, with total sales last year of A$447 million, has the power to push through a change.

But the company's challenge, like others developing similar products, is twofold: to prove synthetic corks work and, more importantly, that they do not in some way retard the ageing process of wine in the bottle.

And they have to convince consumers to accept the end of a centuries-old tradition: natural cork has been used as a wine bottle stopper since the 18th century and is regarded as a perfect seal -- except for the unfortunate problem with taint.
Southcorp estimates taint affects 1.4 billion bottles of wine around the world, or about 10 percent. Cork distributors dispute that, saying the figure is closer to two percent.
According to Mildara's Gregor, cork's big advantage is "the great intangible of romance".

He said the Australian industry was hurt in the 1970s when a move to introduce screw caps -- commonly used for soft drinks and generally regarded as one of the best wine bottle seals around -- provoked a backlash from consumers who insisted that real wine demanded real corks.

With the potential for similar resistance to plastic corks, Jim Humphrys, public relations manager of Australia's second biggest wine producer BRL Hardy, said he believes it would be a mistake to limit synthetic corks to cheaper wines.
"I think the industry has to bite the bullet and put them into some medium-price wines, instead of sending out the signal that they are just for cheap stuff," he said.

Southcorp Wines chief executive Bruce Kemp admits the company, which produces some of Australia's greatest wines including the prized Penfolds Grange Hermitage, has yet to resolve the question of whether synthetic corks could retard the ageing process of premium wines.
It is for that reason, he said, that the company is only testing the Aegis cork, made of food grade polyethylene, in wines which will be drunk fairly quickly, not those left in cellars to age.

Kemp does not believe there will be any problems convincing commercial wine drinkers as long as plastic corks perform as well or better than natural cork, particularly as they are now competitive in price.
"They (synthetic corks) can be opened with a conventional corkscrew, there is still that nice pop at the end of the extraction process," he said.
